section.title: Sing Aloud to God Our Strength
section.sectionRationale: An Asaphite festival psalm that opens in full-voiced praise at a feast, then shifts into God's own first-person address, recalling the Exodus and Meribah, warning against idolatry, and lamenting Israel's refusal to listen, before closing with a wistful promise of finest wheat and honey from the rock.
section.thesis: God still longs to fill the open mouths of His people with the finest provision, but stubborn hearts that will not listen forfeit the very blessings and victories God is eager to give.
section.frameNote: Four movements: the joyful call to feast, 1-3; the festival's memorial of deliverance, 4-7; the solemn warning against idolatry, 8-10; and the sorrow of disobedience answered by the longing promise of blessing, 11-16.

verses.text: Sing for joy to God our strength; make a joyful noise to the God of Jacob.
Lift up a song, strike the tambourine, play the sweet-sounding harp and lyre.
Sound the ram's horn at the New Moon, and at the full moon on the day of our Feast.
For this is a statute for Israel, an ordinance of the God of Jacob.
He ordained it as a testimony for Joseph when he went out over the land of Egypt, where I heard an unfamiliar language:
"I relieved his shoulder of the burden; his hands were freed from the basket.
You called out in distress, and I rescued you; I answered you from the cloud of thunder; I {{nasah|tested}} you at the waters of Meribah. Selah
{{shama|Hear}}, O My people, and I will warn you: O Israel, if only you would listen to Me!
There must be no strange god among you, nor shall you bow to a foreign god.
I am the LORD your God, who brought you up out of Egypt. Open wide your mouth, and I will fill it.

units.label: The sorrow of disobedience, the promise of blessing
units.note: if only, and yet I would

verses.text: But My people would not listen to Me, and Israel would not obey Me.
So I gave them up to their stubborn hearts to follow their own devices.
If only My people would listen to Me, if Israel would follow My ways,
how soon I would subdue their enemies and turn My hand against their foes!
Those who hate the LORD would feign obedience, and their doom would last forever.
But I would feed you the finest wheat; with {{devash|honey}} from the rock I would satisfy you."

shama.gloss: To hear, listen, and obey, a single word covering both attention and response. God's repeated 'if only you would listen' (shama) treats hearing and obeying as one act, not two separate steps.

nasah.gloss: To test or try. At Meribah God tested Israel's trust; the same root elsewhere describes Israel testing God, showing the wilderness as a place where faith or its absence was proven on both sides.

devash.gloss: Honey. God's promised 'honey from the rock' pictures unexpected sweetness supplied from the hardest, driest places, a foretaste of the abundant provision and living water Christ offers, John 4:14, 6:35.

basic.context: This festival psalm opens with full-throated praise at a feast, most likely the Feast of Trumpets or a similar new moon celebration, then shifts to God speaking directly, recalling how He rescued Israel from Egypt and tested them at Meribah. God pleads with His people to listen and forsake other gods, laments that they would not, and closes wistfully with the blessing He still longs to give.
basic.hermeneutics: The psalm moves from celebration to divine oracle to lament, showing worship as the natural setting for hearing God's own voice recall His deeds and press His claims. The repeated 'if only' expresses genuine divine longing for covenant obedience, not resignation.
basic.originalLanguages: God's plea, 'if only you would listen,' uses shama, a word that binds hearing and obeying together as a single act. He recalls testing them, nasah, at Meribah, and promises devash, honey, from the rock, sweetness drawn from the hardest ground, if only they would listen.
basic.typology: The 'finest wheat' and 'honey from the rock' God still longs to give anticipate the far greater provision Christ offers, the bread of life and living water that truly satisfy, John 6:35, 4:14. Israel's testing at Meribah becomes the very episode Hebrews uses to warn believers not to harden their hearts.
basic.christ: Jesus offers Himself as the bread of life, John 6:35, and the living water, John 4:14, the true and final fulfillment of the finest wheat and honey from the rock this psalm holds out. Hebrews 3:7-19 applies the Meribah testing directly as a warning and a call to faith in Christ today.
basic.god: God is shown pleading, not merely commanding, longing for His people's attention and trust, quick to recall His past rescue, painfully honest about giving stubborn hearts over to their own devices, yet still eager, even after refusal, to satisfy His people abundantly.
basic.crossReferences: Hebrews 3:7-19 cites the Meribah testing as a direct warning to trust God today rather than harden the heart. John 6:35 shows Jesus as the bread that truly satisfies, beyond even the finest wheat. Romans 1:24-28 echoes the pattern of God giving people over to their own stubborn hearts.
basic.oneStory: This psalm's ache, God longing to fill wide-open mouths with finest wheat and honey from the rock, while His people refuse to listen, finds its resolution in Christ, the true bread and living water who satisfies all who will finally listen and come to Him.

context.literary:
Psalm 81 falls into two unequal halves with a hinge in the middle of verse 5. Verses 1-5a are the congregation's own voice, a run of imperatives: sing, shout, lift up a song, strike, play, sound the ram's horn. Then, midway through verse 5, the voice changes. 'I heard an unfamiliar language' opens a divine speech that runs to the end of the psalm, verse 16, without another human interruption. The worship leader has stepped aside, and God takes the floor at His own feast.

Inside the oracle the sequence is past, present, then a conditional future. Verses 5b-7 remember the rescue in the first person: the shoulder relieved, the hands freed, the cry answered. Verses 8-10 turn to the present and press the first commandments on the hearers. Verses 11-12 report the failure. Verses 13-16 are a long, unfinished sentence, 'If only... how soon I would... I would feed you,' in which God speaks of what might have been.

The verb of hearing carries the structure. It occurs at verse 5, where the speaker hears a strange language in Egypt, and at verse 8, where God says 'Hear, O My people' and 'if only you would listen.' It returns at verse 11, 'My people would not listen,' and again at verse 13, 'If only My people would listen to Me.' The psalm begins with sound, the horn, tambourine and harp, and turns on the quality of hearing. Loud worship without listening is the psalm's diagnosis. The 'if only' of verse 8 and verse 13 also forms a frame around the sorrowful verses 11-12, so the hardest line of the psalm, 'I gave them up,' sits inside a plea.
context.historical:
The opening verses set the psalm at a feast marked by the ram's horn at the new moon and at the full moon. Trumpets were blown at the start of each month, Numbers 10:10, and the first day of the seventh month was a sacred assembly announced by trumpet blasts, Leviticus 23:24. Fifteen days later, at the full moon of that same month, the Feast of Tabernacles began, Leviticus 23:34. The wording of verse 3 fits that autumn season, when new moon and full moon stood near one another, though the psalm does not name the feast, and it may have been sung at other festivals as well. Jewish tradition later assigned it to a fixed place in the temple worship of the week.

Two features hint at a northern connection. The people are called Joseph and Jacob in verses 1 and 5, names the Asaph collection often uses for the northern tribes, as in Psalm 77:15 and Psalm 80:1. Some think the psalm was brought south after the fall of Samaria, and was sung at a Judean feast in a time of reform. Others place it in the temple worship of Solomon's day. Nothing in the text settles the question.

The oracle draws on Israel's story in Egypt: the shoulder freed of its burden, the hands freed from the basket. The hard labor with brick and mortar in Exodus 1:14 and the promise to bring Israel out from under the burdens of the Egyptians in Exodus 6:6 are the background. The answer 'from the cloud of thunder' recalls Sinai, where God answered Moses in the thunder, Exodus 19:16-19. The test at Meribah is the water from the rock at Rephidim, Exodus 17:1-7, and its later replay at Kadesh, Numbers 20:1-13. The commandments of verses 9-10 are the opening of the Decalogue, Exodus 20:2-3, spoken by God at a feast that was itself a yearly memorial of the rescue.
context.canonical:
Psalm 81 is one of a pair with Psalm 50, another psalm of Asaph in which the LORD calls His people to hear and then confronts them. Psalm 50:7 says, 'Hear, O My people, and I will speak,' and goes on to testify against Israel. Both psalms set covenant worship as the place where God speaks and the people are called to answer with obedience, not merely with sacrifice or song. Psalm 95 is a close relative: it starts with an invitation to sing for joy, then turns to a divine warning, 'Today, if you hear His voice, do not harden your hearts as you did at Meribah,' Psalm 95:7-8.

The text's roots lie in Deuteronomy. The call to hear echoes the Shema, Deuteronomy 6:4, and the honey from the rock and the choicest wheat come from the Song of Moses, Deuteronomy 32:13-14. Prophets pick up the theme of hearing that would have led to peace: 'If only you had paid attention to My commandments, your peace would have been like a river,' Isaiah 48:18, and the picture of stubborn hearts that go their own way appears in Jeremiah 7:24 and Micah 6:16.

The New Testament uses the psalm's setting rather than quoting its words. Hebrews builds a sermon on the Meribah warning, Hebrews 3:7-4:13, and treats 'Today' as a door still open. Paul's account of God giving people over in Romans 1:24-28 has the same structure as verse 12. Stephen tells how God 'gave them over' to worship the heavenly host after the calf, Acts 7:42. And Jesus' words in John 5:40, 'you refuse to come to Me to have life,' and Luke 13:34, 'you were unwilling,' carry the psalm's sorrow into the Gospels.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The author wants worshipers to realize, in the middle of a feast, that God is present as a speaker and not only as an audience. The first three verses build up the noise of the festival. Then God interrupts with a rebuke that is also a plea, and the people are made to hear what is said over their singing. The intention is to bring the joy of worship and the seriousness of obedience together.

The psalm has a specific target, which is the temptation to worship the LORD with instruments and also with a second loyalty. Verse 9 puts it in the negative, 'no strange god among you,' and verse 10 gives the reason: 'I am the LORD your God, who brought you up out of Egypt.' The rescue is not just history; it is the ground of the claim. Anyone who has been brought up from slavery belongs to the One who did it.

Beyond the rebuke the psalm wants to convey how God feels. The line 'If only My people would listen to Me' breaks off without a conclusion, as a person might speak in grief. The author does not soften that pain, and he does not let it be the last word: the final verse holds out the finest wheat and honey from the rock. He wants the hearers to leave the feast both sobered and drawn, aware of the cost of stubbornness and of the generosity still on offer.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The psalm records a festival, a divine speech and a history of refusal. It gives some direct instructions: sing, shout, play, and, in the oracle, hear, have no other god, and open your mouth wide. It does not prescribe every detail of its worship, such as the exact instruments or the timing of the new moon, which belong to Israel's covenant calendar and were fulfilled in Christ, Colossians 2:16-17.

The report in verse 12 that God gave His people up is description of a judgment, not a prescription that anyone should be abandoned. It is a warning, and it should be heard as one. It also does not tell us that every hardship comes from such an abandonment. What it teaches is a pattern: persistent refusal to listen leads God to allow people the results of their own choosing, as Romans 1:24-28 also says.

The prescriptive core is clear. Worship must be joined to listening, since noise and ritual cannot replace obedience. The first commandment stands: no rival to the LORD. And the invitation of verse 10, to open wide and be filled, sets an expectation of receiving from God, not just of giving to Him. Hebrews turns the passage into a present command, 'Today, if you hear His voice, do not harden your hearts,' Hebrews 3:15. So the application is not to reproduce the festival but to hear God's voice and respond to it now.

debates.question: Does 'I gave them up to their stubborn hearts,' verse 12, describe a one-time historical judgment or an ongoing principle of how God deals with persistent refusal?

views.label: A specific historical description of God's response to Israel's wilderness and later unfaithfulness, judged by withholding further intervention at that time
views.case: The immediate context recalls specific past events, Egypt and Meribah, and describes God's response within that history rather than stating a timeless formula. Stephen quotes a similar judgment of God turning away from Israel after the calf, Acts 7:39-42.

views.label: A recurring principle of divine judgment, seen again in Romans 1:24-28, where persistent refusal to listen results in God giving people over to their own chosen path
views.case: Paul's near-identical language in Romans 1 suggests the psalm states a pattern true of God's dealings with hardened hearts in any era, not only ancient Israel's. Proverbs 1:31 says the same: they will be filled with their own devices.

debates.bearing: Both readings agree this is a real and serious act of divine judgment, and both call hearers to listen and obey now rather than presume on future opportunity.

debates.question: Who is speaking in verse 5, 'where I heard an unfamiliar language,' and what does 'he went out over the land of Egypt' mean?

views.label: God is the one who went out over Egypt and heard its foreign speech
views.case: Verse 5 already introduces the divine oracle, and God says at Exodus 11:4, 'About midnight I will go throughout Egypt.' On this reading the LORD Himself recalls walking through a land whose language He heard as strange, in the night He set Joseph free.

views.label: Israel is the speaker, remembering a foreign tongue heard as they left Egypt
views.case: Psalm 114:1 remembers Israel's departure 'from a people of foreign tongue.' On this reading the worshiper's voice is still speaking in verse 5, and God's oracle begins at verse 6, which is where the BSB opens its quotation marks.

debates.bearing: The change of speaker is abrupt in Hebrew and readers have long felt it. What is clear is that the festival is a memorial of Egypt and that the voice of the LORD takes over by verse 6 at the latest.

study.originalLanguages:
Verse 3 calls for the ram's horn at the new moon and 'at the full moon on the day of our Feast.' The Hebrew word for the feast is chag, from a root for a pilgrimage and festival dance, the same word Exodus 12:14 uses for Passover as a feast to the LORD. In verse 4 the feast is said to be a 'statute' and an 'ordinance,' words that belong to law rather than custom. The joy of the day is commanded, and the day itself is a legal sign. Verse 5 calls it a 'testimony,' a word used elsewhere for the tablets and the covenant. A festival is God's own witness to His people of what He did.

In verse 6 the hands are freed from 'the basket.' The Hebrew word is the one for a carrying basket or pot, and here it stands for the forced labor of brickwork and burden-bearing that Exodus 1:14 and Exodus 6:6 describe. The 'burden' of the shoulder is a word for a load carried, the same idea as the burdens God promised to lift.

Verse 7 has God answering 'from the cloud of thunder,' from a Hebrew phrase that means the hidden place of thunder. It ties the answer to Sinai's storm cloud, Exodus 19:16-19, where God responded to Moses in thunder, and the word 'Selah' at the end asks the singers to pause on it. The test at Meribah in this same verse is one of the few places where God is the tester. In Psalm 78:18 and 41 and Psalm 95:8-9 it is Israel who tests God. Here God says, 'I tested you,' and the roles are reversed.

Verse 9 uses two words for outsiders where the BSB has 'strange' and 'foreign' god. The first is the ordinary word for a stranger, the second a word for what is alien. In Deuteronomy 32:12 the same second word appears in 'no foreign god was with him.' The idea is that a god from outside Israel has no place in the household of the LORD.

Verse 10 has two matching verbs: 'open wide' and 'I will fill.' The people are asked to enlarge their mouths, and God promises the filling. The order matters: the need is exposed first. The first half of the verse is Exodus 20:2, the opening of the Ten Commandments, spoken by God at a feast that memorialized the exodus.

In verse 12 God 'gave them up,' with a verb that means sent away or let go, and the result is that they follow their own 'devices,' a word for counsels or schemes, as in Proverbs 1:31. 'Stubborn' is a word that Jeremiah loves to use of the heart, as in Jeremiah 7:24.

Verse 15 says the haters would 'feign obedience.' The verb is related to the word for lying, and it is used of enemies who cower before a stronger power, Psalm 66:3 and Psalm 18:44. It is a forced submission, not real loyalty. The 'doom' that would last forever is literally their time, a word that leaves open what is coming.

Finally the 'finest wheat' of verse 16 is literally the fat of wheat, the best of the grain, a phrase Psalm 147:14 also uses of God's provision, and 'honey from the rock' comes from Deuteronomy 32:13. The sweetness is drawn from hard places.

typology.type: Meribah, where God tested His people, Psalm 81:7
typology.fulfillment: At Rephidim the people quarreled and asked, 'Is the LORD among us or not?' Exodus 17:7. God stood before Moses at the rock, and water came out. Paul reads the rock as Christ: 'they drank from the spiritual rock that accompanied them, and that rock was Christ,' 1 Corinthians 10:4. Jesus, at the feast, cried out, 'If anyone is thirsty, let him come to Me and drink,' John 7:37. The correspondence is that life-giving water comes from a struck source. It escalates because now a Person is the source, and the Spirit is the water, John 7:39. The type falls short because the rock could be tested and forgotten; Christ is the water people are to receive.

typology.type: The feast with trumpets and the memorial of deliverance, Psalm 81:1-5
typology.fulfillment: The festival was a yearly reminder of the Exodus, meant to make each new generation remember what God did. The New Testament sees the feasts as shadows. Colossians 2:16-17 says they are 'a shadow of what is to come; the reality, however, is found in Christ.' Paul says, 'Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed,' 1 Corinthians 5:7, and Jesus did His great invitation at the last day of the Feast of Tabernacles, John 7:37. The correspondence is that a remembered rescue looks to a greater rescue. The type falls short in that a recurring feast cannot itself deliver.

typology.type: The open mouth and the filling, Psalm 81:10, 16
typology.fulfillment: God asks His people to open wide, and He will fill. The finest wheat and honey from the rock are the food of the promised land and of God's generosity. Jesus says, 'I am the bread of life. Whoever comes to Me will never hunger,' John 6:35, and Paul prays that believers be 'filled with all the fullness of God,' Ephesians 3:19. The correspondence is between hunger honestly opened and the satisfaction given. The escalation is that the food is Christ Himself, John 6:51, not merely gifts from the land. The type falls short because wheat and honey feed the body for a day.

typology.type: The unfinished sentence of God's longing, Psalm 81:13-16
typology.fulfillment: The broken 'if only' of God shows a God who grieves over refusal. Jesus speaks in the same voice over Jerusalem: 'how often I have longed to gather your children together as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, but you were unwilling!' Luke 13:34. In the same tone He tells His opponents, 'yet you refuse to come to Me to have life,' John 5:40. The correspondence is the grief of God over a people who will not listen. It escalates in that the longing is now voiced by God in flesh. The type falls short only because in Christ the sentence is finished: the invitation is completed at the cross, and the cry 'Come' goes to every nation, Revelation 22:17.

study.christ:
The psalm leads to Christ first through the voice. God speaks in the first person at His own feast and asks the people to hear. In the Gospels the same voice sounds in Jesus: 'He who has ears to hear, let him hear,' Mark 4:9. At the Transfiguration the Father says of Him, 'Listen to Him,' the psalm's demand transferred to the Son. The listening God asked for at Meribah is now a listening to Jesus. Hebrews brings the two together, quoting the psalm-family warning, 'Today, if you hear His voice, do not harden your hearts,' Hebrews 3:15, and arguing that the same voice now speaks in the Son, Hebrews 1:1-2 and 3:7-4:13. To refuse to hear Christ is to stand in the place of the wilderness generation.

It leads to Christ through the provision. The psalm ends with the promise of the finest wheat and honey from the rock, and the New Testament says that promise has a name. When the crowd asked for bread from heaven, Jesus answered, 'I am the bread of life. Whoever comes to Me will never hunger, and whoever believes in Me will never thirst,' John 6:35. He also stood on the last day of the feast and called out to the thirsty, John 7:37-38. The Meribah rock and the manna both find their answer in one person, and Paul says the rock was Christ, 1 Corinthians 10:4. Isaiah's invitation, 'Listen carefully to Me, and eat what is good,' Isaiah 55:2, echoes the same pairing of hearing and eating.

It leads to Christ through the grief. The unfinished sentence of verse 13, 'If only My people would listen,' is echoed when Jesus weeps over Jerusalem, Luke 19:41-42, and says 'you were unwilling,' Luke 13:34. In Him the divine longing appears in a human voice.

It leads to Christ through the answer to the failure. The people did not listen and God gave them up. Christ, as the true Israel and the perfectly obedient Son, listens where they did not. He is the one who says, 'Not as I will, but as You will,' Matthew 26:39, and by His obedience the disobedient are brought back, Romans 5:19. And the door He opens is real: 'Behold, I stand at the door and knock. If anyone hears My voice and opens the door, I will come in and dine with him,' Revelation 3:20. The psalm's 'open wide your mouth' finds its answer in a Lord who offers a meal.

One caution: the psalm never says that the finest wheat is Christ. It says God longs to feed His people richly, and the New Testament shows the meal is finally Himself. The line runs through the New Testament's own use of bread and water, not through allegory of every detail.
study.god:
The psalm reveals a God who speaks. The whole second half is God's own first-person address, and it reveals a God who does not leave the meaning of the feast to the worshipers. He steps into their singing and tells them what it is for. This is a God who wants to be heard and not only praised.

He is a God who rescues and remembers. 'I relieved his shoulder of the burden; his hands were freed from the basket,' verse 6. The tender specifics, shoulder and hands, show a God who noticed the bodies of slaves. He answered their cry from the thunder, and He does not forget it. Every claim He makes on Israel begins with what He did for them: 'I am the LORD your God, who brought you up out of Egypt,' verse 10.

He is a God who tests and who claims. The test at Meribah is His act, and its purpose, as Deuteronomy 8:2 says, was to know what was in their hearts. His claim is exclusive: no strange god, no foreign god. It rests on love and not on tyranny, because it is joined at once to the offer to fill their mouths.

He is a God who allows people what they choose. Verse 12 states plainly that He gave them up to their stubborn hearts. This is a real judgment, and the psalm's severity should not be blunted. But it is a judgment that comes after long pleading, and it is portrayed as grief. It does not sit alongside any wish to harm. The God of this psalm is so far from enjoying the outcome that He says 'if only' twice.

He is a God of longing. Divine emotion in Scripture is not a weakness. The unfinished sentence of verses 13-16 shows how much He would have done: subdued their enemies, turned His hand against their foes, fed them the finest wheat. His holiness includes an aching wish to bless.

He is a God who is able. The enemies would be subdued in a moment, verse 14, and the food would be the best. Nothing in the picture is beyond His power to give. The only obstacle is the people's ears.

For worship, the psalm tells us to sing with all we have and to be quiet enough to hear. It teaches that our loudest praise means little if we are deaf to what He asks, and that His generosity remains on offer to the one who opens wide.

crossReferences.note: The opening words of the Ten Commandments: 'I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt,' followed by the ban on other gods. Psalm 81:9-10 quotes both halves. At the feast, the covenant is re-announced, with the rescue as its reason.

The water from the rock at Rephidim, named Massah and Meribah because the people tested the LORD by asking whether He was among them. Psalm 81:7 recalls it from God's side, reversing the usual view, since here the LORD says He tested them.

Another festival psalm that opens with joyful singing and turns to a divine warning: 'Today, if you hear His voice, do not harden your hearts as you did at Meribah.' The two psalms share a frame of praise followed by a sober call to listen.

Also a psalm of Asaph, in which God says, 'Hear, O My people, and I will speak, O Israel, and I will testify against you.' Both psalms show God interrupting worship to speak, and both press the point that covenant worship is more than offerings.

The Song of Moses says the LORD alone led Israel, that no foreign god was with him, and that he was nourished with honey from the rock and the choicest grains of wheat. Psalm 81 borrows this language of God's provision and holds it out again.

'If only you had paid attention to My commandments, your peace would have been like a river.' The prophet's 'if only' has the same grief and the same promise as Psalm 81:13-16. A refusal to listen has cost the people peace that God wished to give them.

God says His command was, 'Obey Me, and I will be your God,' but the people followed the stubborn inclinations of their evil hearts. It gives the flavor of Psalm 81:11-12 and shows the phrase was a prophetic commonplace for a people who would not listen.

Stephen tells how the fathers refused to obey, turned back to Egypt in their hearts, made a calf, and how God 'turned away from them and gave them over' to worship the host of heaven. It is the New Testament's commentary on the giving up of Psalm 81:12.

Three times Paul says 'God gave them over' to their desires. The structure matches verse 12: refusal of the truth is answered by God allowing a chosen path. It shows the psalm's principle at work beyond Israel.

The writer builds a sermon on the Meribah warning, asking who heard and rebelled and answering that it was those Moses led out of Egypt. Unbelief kept them out of God's rest. Psalm 81's hearing and not hearing is here turned into a call to believe now.

Jesus says that His Father gives the true bread from heaven, and 'I am the bread of life.' It answers the longing of Psalm 81:16 by naming the food God wanted to give, and shows that hearing and coming to Him is the way to be satisfied.

'Listen carefully to Me, and eat what is good.' The prophet invites the hungry and thirsty to come without money. It is the same pairing of hearing and feeding as in Psalm 81:8 and 16, and it connects the invitation to the everlasting covenant.

study.oneStory:
Psalm 81 takes us to a place the whole Bible keeps returning to: the moment at which a rescued people is asked to listen. The story starts with a God who speaks, and the question of Eden was whether the man and woman would hear and trust His word. Exodus is the story of a God who hears the cry of slaves and answers from the thunder, and Sinai is the moment He speaks the words of the covenant aloud. Psalm 81 places those events inside a feast, so that each generation is brought back to stand at the mountain.

The psalm's warning is the story's recurring tragedy. Israel would not listen at Meribah, and the prophets say the same of the generations that followed, Jeremiah 7:24 and Isaiah 48:18. God's response of giving them up is not a new act but the same sorrowful principle at work in Romans 1 and in Stephen's account in Acts 7. The fall of Samaria and Jerusalem, and the exile that followed, are the long consequence of a people who followed their own counsels.

Yet the psalm ends with something the exile does not cancel: the wistful promise of finest wheat and honey from the rock. The prophets take up the promise. Isaiah 55 calls the thirsty to come and listen and be satisfied on the basis of an everlasting covenant. The promise sits waiting for a people who will finally hear.

The story turns at Christ. He is the Son who listens, the one at whom the Father says 'Listen to Him.' In Him God speaks His last word, Hebrews 1:1-2. He is the bread and the living water, John 6:35 and 7:37-38, the rock that followed the people, 1 Corinthians 10:4. The church, warned by the same history, is told that 'Today' still stands, Hebrews 3:15 and 4:7, and is invited to open wide and receive.

The end of the story is the feast the psalm points toward. In the new creation the thirsty are told, 'Come,' and the one who desires it drinks the water of life freely, Revelation 22:17. Those who overcome eat from the tree of life, Revelation 2:7. The unfinished sentence of Psalm 81 is finished there: the people listen, and God fills their mouths.

sermon.title: Honey from the Rock
sermon.why: Keller preaches directly from Psalm 81, showing how its wilderness imagery, the rock and the honey, points to Jesus, who was tested in the wilderness on our behalf and now satisfies His people through that finished work.

quiz.q: How does the psalm call the congregation to worship, verses 1-3?

options.text: With joyful singing, tambourine, harp, lyre, and the ram's horn at the festival.
options.note: Verses 1-3 list exactly this full-voiced, instrument-filled celebration.

options.text: With complete silence and no instruments.
options.note: The opposite is described; the psalm calls for joyful, loud celebration.

options.text: With mourning rites appropriate to a funeral.
options.note: This is a joyful festival call, not a funeral lament.

options.text: With private, individual prayer only.
options.note: The imagery is thoroughly communal and festive, not solitary.

quiz.q: What does God recall doing for Israel in verses 6-7?

options.text: Relieving their burden in Egypt and rescuing them when they called out in distress.
options.note: Verses 6-7 describe exactly this deliverance.

options.text: Punishing them for leaving Egypt.
options.note: God recalls rescuing them, not punishing their departure.

options.text: Ignoring their cries for help entirely.
options.note: The text says God answered them from the cloud of thunder, not that He ignored them.

options.text: Sending them back into slavery.
options.note: God's action described here is deliverance from slavery, not a return to it.

quiz.q: What warning does God give in verse 9?

options.text: There must be no strange god among them, nor should they bow to a foreign god.
options.note: Verse 9 states this warning directly.

options.text: They must build more temples to various gods.
options.note: The warning is against idolatry, the opposite of building more idol shrines.

options.text: They should stop worshiping altogether.
options.note: The concern is exclusive worship of the LORD, not the end of worship.

options.text: They should worship foreign gods alongside the LORD.
options.note: The verse explicitly forbids any foreign god, not a shared worship arrangement.

quiz.q: How did Israel actually respond to God's plea to listen, verse 11?

options.text: My people would not listen to Me, and Israel would not obey Me.
options.note: Verse 11 states this refusal directly.

options.text: They listened perfectly and obeyed every command.
options.note: The text states the opposite, a refusal to listen and obey.

options.text: They listened but forgot within a single day.
options.note: The text describes an outright refusal to listen, not a brief lapse.

options.text: They listened only when it was convenient for them.
options.note: The verse states a general refusal, not selective or conditional listening.

quiz.q: What is God's longed-for promise in verse 16, if His people would only listen?

options.text: He would feed them the finest wheat and satisfy them with honey from the rock.
options.note: This is the exact promise of verse 16, fulfilled ultimately in Christ.

options.text: He would remove all festivals and celebrations.
options.note: The promise is abundant provision, not the removal of worship.

options.text: He would give them over permanently to their enemies.
options.note: This is the opposite of the promised blessing; that fate belongs to those who hate the LORD, verse 15.

options.text: He would delay any blessing indefinitely.
options.note: The promise is immediate and abundant, 'how soon,' verse 14, not indefinitely delayed.

questions: The psalm opens in full-voiced festival praise, verses 1-3. What would it look like for your own worship, whether alone or with others, to be marked by that same wholehearted joy?
God recalls relieving Israel's burden and rescuing them when they cried out, verses 6-7. What burden has God already relieved in your life that you need to remember today?
God pleads, 'if only you would listen to Me,' verses 8, 13. Where is God currently asking for your attention and obedience, and what is keeping you from listening fully?
Verse 12 shows the real cost of persistent refusal, being given over to one's own stubborn heart. Where might you be experiencing the painful freedom of getting exactly what you insisted on?

God still longs to fill wide-open mouths with the finest wheat and honey from the rock, verse 16, fulfilled in Christ, the bread of life. What would it mean this week to come to Jesus with your mouth, and your life, wide open?

translationNotes.note: 'Gittith,' in the psalm's heading, likely names a melody or instrument, possibly brought from the Philistine city of Gath; it appears also in the headings of Psalms 8 and 84.
'An unfamiliar language' recalls Israel's time in Egypt among a foreign tongue, underscoring how far God reached to rescue His people from genuine bondage.
'Meribah' means quarreling or strife, naming the place, Exodus 17:7, where Israel tested God over water, an episode Hebrews 3 later uses as a direct warning to believers.
